screens.title: Player input: the role it plays
screens.narratorSegment: Player input is the set of signals coming from devices—keyboard, mouse, gamepad—that tell the game what the player intends. In Unity, the legacy Input class and Input Manager together let your game read those signals each frame and interpret them as movement, actions, or UI events. Defining named axes and virtual buttons in the Input Manager decouples the physical device from game code: instead of checking for a specific KeyCode throughout your project you query a meaningful name like "Horizontal" or "Jump". This makes controls remappable and lets multiple devices drive the same behavior. A concrete example: map both A/D keys and a gamepad left stick X-axis to the "Horizontal" axis. Your movement code reads a single float and works for both keyboard and controller. A common misconception is thinking Input only reports instantaneous events; in fact some methods like GetKey return a continuous state while GetKeyDown returns a single-frame event—choosing the wrong one changes play feel. The takeaway: treat input names as public A P I for player intent and use the Input Manager to keep that A P I device-agnostic. How would you map sprint, crouch, and fire so they work across keyboard and gamepad?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Core Concept

What is player input?

Signals from devices interpreted by your game as movement, actions, or UI commands. Input Manager maps device inputs to named axes and buttons.

Definition

Input reports player intent. Treat those named inputs as the API your gameplay code reads every frame.

Analogy

Think of Input Manager as a translator that converts keyboard and joystick into a single language for your code.

Common mistake

Hardcoding KeyCodes throughout your scripts makes remapping and controller support painful.

Concrete example

Map A/D and left stick X to "Horizontal". Code reads Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") and moves the character without caring which device produced the value.
Takeaway
Name inputs by intent, not by device. That keeps your gameplay code clear and portable.
Try this
Create a virtual button "Fire" and assign left mouse and gamepad trigger to it in Input Manager.

screens.title: Keyboard input: GetKey, GetKeyDown, GetKeyUp
screens.narratorSegment: Unity exposes three primary keyboard query methods that you will use frequently: GetKey, GetKeyDown, and GetKeyUp. GetKey returns true as long as the key is held; use it for continuous actions like moving or sprinting. GetKeyDown returns true only during the frame the key is first pressed, making it ideal for single-press actions such as jumping or opening a menu. GetKeyUp fires on the frame the key is released and can be useful for actions that should trigger on release, such as cancelling a charge attack. A common error for beginners is using GetKey for actions that should occur only once. For example, if you use GetKey to trigger a jump you will repeatedly apply jump logic while the key is held, producing multiple jumps. The concrete example in this lesson shows a script snippet that checks Input. GetKey(KeyCode. W) for forward movement and Input. GetKeyDown(KeyCode. Space) to add an impulse for a single jump. Always pair the single-press check with a grounded check so a single press yields one jump. Does your jump fire once or repeatedly when you test it?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Definition

GetKey family

Pick the method that matches the expected timing: hold vs press vs release.

GetKey

Returns true while a key is held. Good for movement and sustained actions.

GetKeyDown

True only on the frame the key is first pressed. Use for jumps, firing single-shot events, or toggles.

GetKeyUp

True on the frame the key is released. Useful for release-triggered behaviors.

Sample snippet

// Movement input (continuous)
if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W))
{
  // Move forward while held
}

// Jump input (single-press)
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) && isGrounded)
{
  // Apply jump impulse once
}
Concrete tip
Always check grounded state when using GetKeyDown for jumping to ensure one jump per press.
Check your understanding
If your character jumps repeatedly while you hold the jump key, which method are you likely using incorrectly?

screens.title: Mouse input and mousePosition
screens.narratorSegment: Mouse input in Unity follows the same holding vs single-frame pattern as keyboard input, but uses integer button indices. Use GetMouseButton(0) for the left mouse while the button is held, GetMouseButtonDown(0) for detecting the exact frame of a click, and GetMouseButtonUp(0) for release events. These methods are useful for weapon firing, dragging UI elements, or measuring click duration. Another important mouse value is Input. mousePosition, which returns the cursor's pixel coordinates as a Vector3 where z is zero. You use mousePosition to project screen-space coordinates into the scene for raycasts or camera-based aiming. A concrete example: on left click you might spawn a projectile at the cursor's world position by converting mousePosition with a Camera. ScreenPointToRay and a Physics. Raycast. A common misconception is expecting mouse X/Y axes to be directly the same as Input. GetAxis("Mouse X") or GetAxisRaw; those axes report movement deltas rather than absolute screen position. The key takeaway: choose the right mouse method for the interaction you want—click detection, hold, release, or absolute position for aiming. Mouse input and mousePosition means use mouse button methods for clicks and input.mouseposition for cursor coordinates when mapping screen input to world actions.. In practical terms, buttons, clicks, and cursor coordinates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Mouse Input

Mouse buttons and position

Left, right, and middle buttons use indices 0, 1, and 2. Use the holding and single-frame methods by index.

GetMouseButton

True while a mouse button is held. Good for dragging or continuous fire.

GetMouseButtonDown

True on the frame the button is pressed. Use to detect a single click event.

Input.mousePosition

Returns the cursor pixel position as a Vector3. Convert it to world coordinates before spawning objects.

Concrete scenario

On left click detect screen point via mousePosition, cast a ray into the scene, and place an object where the ray hits the ground. Use GetMouseButtonDown for a single placement per click.
Misconception
Mouse X and Mouse Y axes report movement deltas, not absolute screen coordinates—use mousePosition for absolute position.
Key Takeaway
Pick index-based methods for click behavior and mousePosition for cursor-to-world conversions.

screens.title: Input Manager and named axes
screens.narratorSegment: The Input Manager maps multiple physical inputs to named axes and virtual buttons so your code can read a single name and respond consistently. Built-in axes include Horizontal and Vertical for movement and Mouse X and Mouse Y for pointer motion. Each axis entry in the Input Manager has properties like Positive Button, Negative Button, Alt Positive Button, Alt Negative Button, Gravity, Sensitivity, and Type. Gravity and Sensitivity control smoothing: gravity dictates how quickly the value returns to zero when the input ends, sensitivity affects how rapidly the value reaches its target. Type selects Key or Mouse Button, Mouse Movement, or Joystick Axis. The typical workflow is: open Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager, find the axis entry, and add alternate keys or assign a joystick axis. A practical example: add Joystick Axis as an alt for a Horizontal axis so both keyboard A/D and a gamepad stick drive the same axis. A common novice mistake is tuning gravity and sensitivity too aggressively, producing sluggish or overly abrupt movement. The takeaway: use the manager to compose inputs by intent and tune properties for the play feel you want.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Process Flow

How to map an axis

Follow this process to create or tune a named axis that supports multiple devices.
  1. Open Input Manager: Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager and expand Axes.
  2. Select or add an entry: Use an existing axis like "Horizontal" or duplicate to create a custom axis such as "FireAxis".
  3. Assign buttons/axes: Set Positive Button, Negative Button, and Alt buttons or Joystick Axis for controller support.
  4. Tune smoothing: Set Gravity and Sensitivity to control how the value ramps and returns to zero.
  5. Test in Play mode: Verify keyboard and gamepad both produce the expected values in your movement code.

Axis properties explained

Gravity: how quickly input returns to neutral when released.
Sensitivity: how fast the axis value ramps toward its target.
Type: Key/Mouse Button, Mouse Movement, or Joystick Axis.
Example
Map A/D and joystick X to Horizontal so the same code moves the player for both devices.

screens.title: GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides two ways to read axis values: GetAxis and GetAxisRaw. GetAxis returns a smoothed floating value between -1 and 1, applying gravity and sensitivity to create a gradual ramping effect. This smoothing often feels more natural for character movement because acceleration and deceleration are softened. GetAxisRaw, by contrast, returns the immediate device value—typically -1, 0, or 1 for digital inputs—without smoothing. Use GetAxisRaw when you want instant responses such as pixel-perfect movement, tight platforming controls, or when you implement your own custom filtering. An example: read Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") for a camera that eases into motion, but use Input. GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") when your game requires crisp tile-based movement. A common pitfall is mixing smoothed axes with physics code that expects instantaneous input; smoothing can cause unexpected forces if not accounted for. The takeaway: choose smoothed or raw based on whether you want interpolation built into the input or direct, immediate values you will process yourself. GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw means use getaxis for natural-feeling, smoothed movement and getaxisraw for instant controls that need no built-in interpolation.. In practical terms, smoothing, responsiveness, and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Comparison

GetAxis (smoothed)

Automatically interpolates values using axis Gravity and Sensitivity for a softer feel.

Good for natural-feeling movement and camera panning that should ease in and out.

GetAxisRaw (unsmoothed)

Returns the raw input value immediately with no smoothing, useful for precise controls.

Good for pixel-perfect movement or when you implement your own acceleration model.
Example
Use GetAxis for third-person walking, GetAxisRaw for immediate left/right tile steps.
Pitfall
Smoothed axes combined with physics velocity changes can feel laggy if not tuned properly.
Takeaway
Pick smoothing based on the control responsiveness your game needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Code Walkthrough

PlayerController essentials

Use Rigidbody for physics movement and GetButtonDown for jump input. Preserve Y velocity when applying X/Z movement.

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f;
  public float jumpForce = 8f;

  private Rigidbody rb;
  private bool isGrounded = true;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
    if (rb == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("Rigidbody not found on PlayerController object!");
      enabled = false;
    }
  }

  void Update()
  {
    float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    float verticalInput = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

    Vector3 moveDirection = transform.right * horizontalInput + transform.forward * verticalInput;
    moveDirection.Normalize();

    rb.velocity = new Vector3(moveDirection.x * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y, moveDirection.z * moveSpeed);

    if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
    {
      rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
      isGrounded = false;
    }
  }

  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
  {
    if (collision.contacts.Length > 0)
    {
      Vector3 normal = collision.contacts[0].normal;
      if (Vector3.Dot(normal, Vector3.up) > 0.7f)
      {
        isGrounded = true;
      }
    }
  }
}

  • Place Plane at Y = 0 and ensure collisions are enabled.
  • Run Play mode and press W/A/S/D or arrow keys to move, Space to jump.

screens.title: Common mistakes & migration hint
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes that can frustrate beginners. First, confusing GetButton with GetButtonDown results in repeated triggers when you expect single actions like opening an inventory. GetButton returns true while a button is held; GetButtonDown returns true only on the initial frame. Second, hardcoding KeyCodes across many scripts makes remapping and controller support costly. Third, mixing transform-based movement with Rigidbody physics leads to collision and stability problems. When should you consider the newer Input System? The legacy Input Manager is simple and fine for many single-player prototypes. The new Input System is action-based, event-driven, and better suited when you need multiple control schemes, local multiplayer, or advanced gamepad features. Use the legacy system first to learn core concepts, and migrate when your project requires multi-device action maps, rebinding at runtime, or richer device support. The takeaway: start simple, avoid the three common mistakes, and plan to move to the new Input System when your control requirements exceed the legacy manager's capabilities. Scene setup steps

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll treat player input as the bridge between the person at the keyboard and the objects in your 3D world. You'll learn the core patterns of Unity's legacy Input system so you can read keys, mouse buttons, axes, and virtual buttons and turn those signals into movement, jumps, and in-game actions. We'll look at the Input class methods you will call from Update, how Input Manager axes let you abstract keyboard and gamepad controls into a single name, and the difference between continuous input and single-press input. You'll also see a complete PlayerController script that moves a cube with Horizontal/Vertical axes and triggers jumps using the Jump virtual button. Finally, we'll briefly mention the newer Input System package so you know when to consider upgrading for more complex control schemes. By the end of the module you will be able to wire basic controls, avoid common input bugs, and configure remappable axes in the Input Manager.

These four objectives will prepare you to read player input reliably and design flexible controls. First, you'll understand the core principles of player input in Unity: what the Input class reports, how frames affect button state, and why separating continuous and single-press actions matters. Second, you'll use the legacy Input Manager to detect keyboard keys, mouse buttons, and mouse movement; this gives you a concrete way to map physical devices into named axes and buttons. Third, you'll implement C# scripts that respond to continuous input like movement and to single-press input like jumping, including a simple Rigidbody-based PlayerController example. Fourth, you'll learn to map custom input axes and virtual buttons in the Input Manager so your controls can be remapped without changing code. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual idea so you remember to keep input names abstract and behavior-specific. These skills let you make controls that are responsive, remappable, and easy to test.

These additional objectives complete your roadmap for practical input handling. First, you'll be introduced to the newer Input System package so you know when to choose it over the legacy manager; the course focuses on the legacy system but you'll learn the reason to consider an action-based input system for complex games. Second, you'll identify common mistakes such as confusing GetButton with GetButtonDown and learn how those mistakes change behaviour in a running game. Third, you'll complete a hands-on activity: set up a scene with a Cube and Plane, attach a Rigidbody and write a PlayerController script that uses Horizontal and Vertical axes for movement and Jump for a single-press jump. Fourth, you'll practice inspecting the Input Manager's axis entries and understand properties like Positive Button, Alt Positive Button, Gravity, Sensitivity, and Type for better tuning. These objectives include a small mnemonic so you remember to use named inputs for remapping and to avoid hardcoding KeyCodes everywhere.

Player input is the set of signals coming from devices—keyboard, mouse, gamepad—that tell the game what the player intends. In Unity, the legacy Input class and Input Manager together let your game read those signals each frame and interpret them as movement, actions, or UI events. Defining named axes and virtual buttons in the Input Manager decouples the physical device from game code: instead of checking for a specific KeyCode throughout your project you query a meaningful name like "Horizontal" or "Jump". This makes controls remappable and lets multiple devices drive the same behavior. A concrete example: map both A/D keys and a gamepad left stick X-axis to the "Horizontal" axis. Your movement code reads a single float and works for both keyboard and controller. A common misconception is thinking Input only reports instantaneous events; in fact some methods like GetKey return a continuous state while GetKeyDown returns a single-frame event—choosing the wrong one changes play feel. The takeaway: treat input names as public A P I for player intent and use the Input Manager to keep that A P I device-agnostic. How would you map sprint, crouch, and fire so they work across keyboard and gamepad?

Unity exposes three primary keyboard query methods that you will use frequently: GetKey, GetKeyDown, and GetKeyUp. GetKey returns true as long as the key is held; use it for continuous actions like moving or sprinting. GetKeyDown returns true only during the frame the key is first pressed, making it ideal for single-press actions such as jumping or opening a menu. GetKeyUp fires on the frame the key is released and can be useful for actions that should trigger on release, such as cancelling a charge attack. A common error for beginners is using GetKey for actions that should occur only once. For example, if you use GetKey to trigger a jump you will repeatedly apply jump logic while the key is held, producing multiple jumps. The concrete example in this lesson shows a script snippet that checks Input. GetKey(KeyCode. W) for forward movement and Input. GetKeyDown(KeyCode. Space) to add an impulse for a single jump. Always pair the single-press check with a grounded check so a single press yields one jump. Does your jump fire once or repeatedly when you test it?

Mouse input in Unity follows the same holding vs single-frame pattern as keyboard input, but uses integer button indices. Use GetMouseButton(0) for the left mouse while the button is held, GetMouseButtonDown(0) for detecting the exact frame of a click, and GetMouseButtonUp(0) for release events. These methods are useful for weapon firing, dragging UI elements, or measuring click duration. Another important mouse value is Input. mousePosition, which returns the cursor's pixel coordinates as a Vector3 where z is zero. You use mousePosition to project screen-space coordinates into the scene for raycasts or camera-based aiming. A concrete example: on left click you might spawn a projectile at the cursor's world position by converting mousePosition with a Camera. ScreenPointToRay and a Physics. Raycast. A common misconception is expecting mouse X/Y axes to be directly the same as Input. GetAxis("Mouse X") or GetAxisRaw; those axes report movement deltas rather than absolute screen position. The key takeaway: choose the right mouse method for the interaction you want—click detection, hold, release, or absolute position for aiming. Mouse input and mousePosition means use mouse button methods for clicks and input.mouseposition for cursor coordinates when mapping screen input to world actions.. In practical terms, buttons, clicks, and cursor coordinates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Input Manager maps multiple physical inputs to named axes and virtual buttons so your code can read a single name and respond consistently. Built-in axes include Horizontal and Vertical for movement and Mouse X and Mouse Y for pointer motion. Each axis entry in the Input Manager has properties like Positive Button, Negative Button, Alt Positive Button, Alt Negative Button, Gravity, Sensitivity, and Type. Gravity and Sensitivity control smoothing: gravity dictates how quickly the value returns to zero when the input ends, sensitivity affects how rapidly the value reaches its target. Type selects Key or Mouse Button, Mouse Movement, or Joystick Axis. The typical workflow is: open Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager, find the axis entry, and add alternate keys or assign a joystick axis. A practical example: add Joystick Axis as an alt for a Horizontal axis so both keyboard A/D and a gamepad stick drive the same axis. A common novice mistake is tuning gravity and sensitivity too aggressively, producing sluggish or overly abrupt movement. The takeaway: use the manager to compose inputs by intent and tune properties for the play feel you want.

Unity provides two ways to read axis values: GetAxis and GetAxisRaw. GetAxis returns a smoothed floating value between -1 and 1, applying gravity and sensitivity to create a gradual ramping effect. This smoothing often feels more natural for character movement because acceleration and deceleration are softened. GetAxisRaw, by contrast, returns the immediate device value—typically -1, 0, or 1 for digital inputs—without smoothing. Use GetAxisRaw when you want instant responses such as pixel-perfect movement, tight platforming controls, or when you implement your own custom filtering. An example: read Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") for a camera that eases into motion, but use Input. GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") when your game requires crisp tile-based movement. A common pitfall is mixing smoothed axes with physics code that expects instantaneous input; smoothing can cause unexpected forces if not accounted for. The takeaway: choose smoothed or raw based on whether you want interpolation built into the input or direct, immediate values you will process yourself. GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw means use getaxis for natural-feeling, smoothed movement and getaxisraw for instant controls that need no built-in interpolation..
